sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for?** No.
   - **Where:** the top band (0–55 px) and the whole column at 160–980 px.
   - **What the viewer meets:** there is no page title, no bakery name and no "Help" or "Questions about your order" label. A viewer has to read two or three topics before working out that these are answers about collecting a bakery pre-order. Even then they can't tell which bakery or which service.
   - **Why:** Krug (*Don't Make Me Think*) says a page should be self-evident. Here the purpose is only inferable, not stated.
   - **Fix:** add one title above the list, such as "Collecting your order: common questions", and name the bakery or service somewhere nearby. If this capture is a section cut from a longer page that already has that title, the finding goes away.
   - **Kind and weight:** convention, minor.

Outside the checklist (copy, weighed by what the viewer acts on):

2. **"Orders can be cancelled up to a day ahead"** (y≈416).
   - **Problem:** "ahead" of what? It could mean 24 hours before the pickup time, or by the end of the day before pickup day. This is a deadline the customer will hold the bakery to, so the wrong reading means a customer who thinks they cancelled in time, or a refund dispute.
   - **Fix:** state the cut-off exactly, e.g. "You can cancel until 24 hours before your pickup time", and keep "after that we've already baked your bread" as the reason.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, major for this topic.
3. **"along with a name"** (y≈217).
   - **Problem:** it's unclear whose name: the collector's own or the person who placed the order. Someone collecting for a friend may turn up with the wrong one.
   - **Fix:** say which name, e.g. "along with the name the order was placed under".
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, minor.
4. **"The bakery holds orders for two hours after the chosen time"** (y≈104–131).
   - **Problem:** the line states the policy but stops before the consequence: what happens to the viewer's order after two hours?
   - **Fix:** finish the line in the viewer's terms, e.g. "…after that, it goes back on the shelf."
   - **Kind and weight:** taste, minor.

**What's working.**
- **One voice throughout.** One typeface, one ink color, one left edge and a plain friendly tone make it read as a single calm, trustworthy help page. Nothing is decorative, and no element could come out without loss.
- **Specific headings.** Each heading names a real situation in the customer's own words ("Collecting for someone else", "Cancelling an order"), so someone scanning finds their question without reading the answers.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (first-time viewer can say what it's for).

I read the whole image directly rather than in crops (Bash was refused, and the image is about one screen). For the deep read I opened `references/art-direction.md` with Read, but only its first 120 lines, so I didn't see the entries named by the "no" line.

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. The four headings ("Changing your pickup time" at y≈69, "Collecting for someone else" at y≈182, "Allergies and ingredients" at y≈268, "Cancelling an order" at y≈381, all at x=160) are in the same face, weight and near-black colour as the answers below them. They also look one or two pixels *smaller* than the answer text, so they read as weaker than what they introduce. The only thing that marks them as headings is the small gap of about 10 px under each one. Someone scanning for their question, such as "can I cancel?", has to read the first line of every block to find it, so the page loses the one thing an FAQ is for. It also reads as a flat run of eight paragraphs rather than four question-and-answer pairs. The reason is Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8 and 8a–8g: when two elements are meant to differ, the difference has to be obvious at a glance, and a heading within a pixel or two of its text, or in the same size, weight and colour, is the worst case the "Weak contrast is worse than none" entry describes. *Fix:* give each heading a difference you see at a glance. The simplest move is bold or semibold at the same size or one clear step up. A clearly darker or brighter body/heading colour split would also work. Don't leave the heading smaller than the body. Marked **defect**, weight **major**.
2. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No. The page has no title and no element larger or heavier than the rest. The eye lands top-left at (160, 69) only because of reading order, and nothing tells the viewer what page this is (pickup help, order FAQ) before they start reading. The reason is Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*: when elements compete at equal weight, the eye has no anchor. *Fix:* add a page title that clearly dominates, such as "Pickup and orders", well above the heading size and set apart by weight. That gives the viewer a starting point and a frame for the four questions. Marked **defect**, weight **major** if this block stands alone as a page, and minor if a page title sits above the captured area. The image shows about 60 px of empty space above the first heading and nothing else.

**What's working.** The spacing does some of the grouping work. Each heading sits closer to its own answer (gap of about 10 px) than to the answer above it (about 30–40 px), so the four pairs still read as pairs even without type contrast. Keep that rhythm when you add weight to the headings.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 1 yes, 2 no (one element stands clearly above the rest; each level of the text distinguishable at a glance), 0 unsure

Fair to say: arrangement isn't where this page has problems. Spacing and alignment do their job. The one finding is small and is my own view.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion, such as halves, thirds, or the golden section, rather than arbitrary splits?** The text column runs from x≈160 to x≈980 on a frame about 1280 px wide. That splits the width into about 160 : 820 : 300, which matches no proportion and no other edge on the page. The column's center (x≈570) sits about 70 px left of the frame's center (x≈640). That is too far off to read as a mistake in centering, but not far enough to read as a clear choice to hang the column left. The viewer sees a column that looks like a container with a maximum width parked against the left margin. It also leaves a bare 300 px band down the right side. With the content ending at y≈430, the lower 370 px are empty too, so the content clusters in the top-left of the screen. The cost to someone reading the answers is small. Direction: either center the column so the side margins match, or make the left hang clearly deliberate, by lining it up with the site's header and navigation grid or by putting the questions in a narrow left column of their own. Then both side margins would come from one rule. Taste (judged as a designer; the checklist itself warns against relying on golden-section rules, so I cite no published one). Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The gaps group the items correctly. Each question sits about 10 px above its answer, and each answer ends about 38 px before the next question. That is roughly a 1 : 4 ratio, so each question clearly belongs to its own answer, and the four pairs read as four separate items without any rules or boxes (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II, on proximity). Keep this ratio if you change the type.
- Everything lines up on one edge. Every question and answer starts exactly at x=160 with no near-misses, so the eye drops straight down the list. The empty space is collected into one area at the bottom and right rather than scattered between items.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (main divisions of the frame follow one proportion).

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters? No.** The answers run to the edge of a column about 820 px wide (x 160–980). "Give the person your order number… along with a name." (y 217) and "Orders can be cancelled… baked for you." (y 416) are about 95 characters each, and the first answer's line (y 104) is about 89. Most answers are only one or two lines, so the reader seldom has to find the start of the next line. The cost is that one-line answers become long strips that are slow to take in, and each question sits far from the end of its answer. Bringhurst (*Elements*, 2.1.2) gives 45–75 characters as comfortable. Fix: narrow the text column to about 600–640 px at this size, roughly 65–70 characters. The page has plenty of empty space on the right and below. *Convention. Weight: minor.*
2. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line? No.** "anything." sits alone on the last line of the allergies answer (y 330), and the word carries no weight there. The first answer also ends on a short "after the chosen time." (y 131). Together they make a ragged, spotty right side in an otherwise quiet block. Bringhurst (*Elements*, 2.4.2). Fix: the narrower measure from finding 1 will rewrap both. Then check the last lines again and use balanced wrapping or a non-breaking space so that no single word is left alone. *Convention. Weight: minor.*
3. **The copy (no checklist line; my judgment).** "They will need to show it at the counter along with a name" (y 217) can be read two ways. It could mean the collector's own name or the name the order was placed under. A customer who sends a friend could get this wrong and have the friend turned away at the till. Fix: name which one, e.g. "…along with the name the order is under." "Orders can be cancelled up to a day ahead" (y 416) is a deadline, and "a day ahead" could mean 24 hours before the pickup slot or any time the day before. Fix: give the cutoff exactly, e.g. "until 24 hours before your pickup time." *Defect. Weight: major for the cancellation line, because people hold the business to deadlines. Minor for the name line.*

Note for the director, outside this section: the questions (y 69, 182, 268, 381) look about 18 px and regular weight. That is slightly smaller than the 19 px answers and only a little different in colour, so headings and answers read as one level. This belongs to Hierarchy/type scale, not here.

**What's working.** One plain sans in near-black on white, with ample size and contrast. Nothing gets in the way of reading. The space between items (about 35 px) is clearly larger than the space between a question and its answer (about 12 px), so each question stays grouped with its answer even though the type doesn't separate them.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters; clean breaks with no lone short word)

**Walk (working notes)**

The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image without crops. First read: a plain FAQ or help list for a bakery's ordering service. There are four short question-and-answer pairs in near-black on white, set in one left column. The eye starts at "Changing your pickup time" and reads straight down. It feels calm and plain. There are no hues anywhere.

Job (my assumption): a help section that answers customers' practical questions about picking up and cancelling orders.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. It uses one neutral, near-black on white.
- Saturated color kept to a small share of the area: yes. There is no saturated color.
- Clear range of light and dark that still shows the structure in grayscale: yes. Dark text on white is the full range. Headings and answers share one dark value, so the split between them rests on size and spacing. That belongs to hierarchy, not color.
- Warm colors forward, cool colors back: yes. There are no hues.
- Colors meant to match look the same everywhere: yes. Text color is the same across all eight blocks.
- Neighbouring strong colors differ clearly in lightness: yes. There are no neighbouring strong colors.
- Status colors used only for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by color alone: yes. No meaning is carried by color.
- Dark theme uses dark gray rather than pure black: yes. It is a light theme, so this does not apply.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so I opened no entries.

---

**Section.** Color: applies. The piece is all neutral (near-black text on white), so the section is short.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The text looks like a very dark gray rather than pure black on white. That keeps the contrast high for a dense block of body copy without the harsh glare of pure black on white. Using one value for all text also means nothing competes for color attention, which suits a plain help list. If the headings ever need to stand apart from the answers, color is one option: make the answers a lighter gray, not the headings a hue. That choice belongs to the hierarchy critic.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
